title: Ivan Smirnov
text: Everyone, Let me start your day with some irony and some food for thought: As you may know, these days it is possible to run decent LLMs locally on your desktop machine. All you need is a decent GPU. Here is what I did recently and what that led to: 1. I installed Ollama and the latest Qwen LLM from Alibaba. Qwen is meant to handle advanced coding tasks, among other things. Installation was smooth and simple. (Don't worry, I created a blocking outbound rule in my firewall.) ;-) 2. As an initial test, I asked Qwen to 'explain race conditions' to me as if I was a C# developer (which I am). I could briefly see some text coming up, and then everything died. My screens went black. No warnings. All dead. In the end, only a full-blown extra hard power reset got my machine up and running again. I haven't had to do that in 5 years. Then I tried the same thing again. Same result. Badly dead machine. =/ =/ =/ =/ =/ =/ =/ =/ =/ =/ =/ =/ =/ =/ =/ =/ The irony was clear (and when asked, Claude agreed): Running an LLM draws *lots* of power. That is why data centers are like black holes for electricity. Running a local LLM on a local GPU is no different. My local GPU needed lots of power very suddenly and the power supply in my local machine may never have experienced such a power spike, even compared to running demanding games. LLMs draw so much power that surrounding societies and systems may suffer. They want all the power you have - and more. Today, I got to experience that first-hand. Take care, everyone! /Björn
author: Ivan Smirnov

title: Ivan Smirnov • 1-й
text: Hi everyone! I’ve written a new article about an approach I’ve been using to work with AI agents as a team rather than as isolated autonomous agents. Different agents take on tasks with different levels of complexity, communicate with each other, share findings and build on each other’s work. I thought this approach might be useful for others working on complex AI-driven workflows. Three months ago, I wrote about the challenges that emerged when autonomous AI agents started operating in orchestrator mode: false positives, drift, verification, orchestration and operational stability. Since then, my approach has evolved again. I gradually moved from individual autonomous agents and a centralized orchestrator to agent teams, where agents don’t simply execute tasks in parallel. They share results, warn each other about discovered issues and use previous findings to shape the next experiments. For me, the biggest shift is from: “The agent thinks this will improve performance.” to: “We tested it, measured it, and here is the evidence.” In this article, I’ll break down this approach using a real performance optimization case involving a customer pipeline with around 40 pods, each responsible for a different part of the processing. I’ll show how I split the work between multiple agents, how they communicate findings and hypotheses, how they run experiments in a real test environment, and how the workflow moves from AI-generated recommendations to evidence-based optimization. And this is where performance optimization is particularly interesting: the result is something you can actually see and measure. Here is the baseline solution. Here is the optimized solution. The same data. The same infrastructure. The same workload. And here is the difference in execution time. Instead of saying that an optimization should improve performance, I can actually measure how much it improved it. #ai #ai_automation
author: Ivan Smirnov • 1-й

title: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. • Отслеживаете
text: NODA AI went from a $10M contract to orchestrate drone swarms for one program (LUCAS) to a $100M contract to scale that same layer across the Joint Force — in roughly a month. That's not typical, and it's not just a good sales quarter. A single-program pilot and an enterprise-wide deployment are different technical problems. The pilot has to prove the orchestration works for one customer's platforms, one mission set, one integration point. The enterprise version has to work when the next platform added wasn't in the original design — different manufacturer, different data model, different failure mode — without a rewrite. You can't retrofit that extensibility after the fact, not on a government timeline. It has to be a decision made before the first contract: is the boundary between "my orchestration logic" and "the platform I'm orchestrating" narrow, versioned, and well-documented — or is it whatever got the pilot working fastest? The former costs more up front and looks identical in the pilot demo. It's also the only version that survives the jump from single-program funding to enterprise-wide funding without a full re-architecture in between. I've sat across the table from small autonomy companies working through exactly that tradeoff — whether to optimize for the current SBIR deliverable or for the interface that has to survive three more customers after it. It's rarely obvious in the moment which one you're doing. Worth deciding on purpose rather than by default. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy
